articles.title: First images of the impact of DART asteroid deflection experiment
articles.content: Four years ago, NASA dispatched a small spacecraft on a suicide mission to show how humanity might deflect an asteroid on a collision course with Earth. The first-of-its-kind experiment worked beautifully as the solar-powered space probe slammed into asteroid Dimorphos, permanently altering its trajectory. Using telescopes, astronomers measured changes in the orbit of Dimorphos around a larger asteroid companion named Didymos in the aftermath of NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) mission. The spacecraft released some 10 billion joules of energy as it impacted Dimorphos in September 2022 at more than 13,700 mph (6.14 kilometers per second), shortening the asteroid’s 12-hour orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, 25 times the most conservative expectation. But scientists could only learn so much from DART. The collision destroyed the spacecraft, as expected. DART recorded images as it took aim on Dimorphos, but only faraway telescopes and a small CubeSat that briefly detected the impact flash could see what happened next. “We knew right away that the impact was successful, that DART made a really, really large mess,” said Sabina Raducan, a planetary scientist at the International Space Science Institute in Bern, Switzerland. “However, we didn’t really know what kind of mess. We were still missing pieces of the puzzle.” Artist’s illustration of the Hera spacecraft with its two deployable CubeSats, Juventas and Milani, in the vicinity of the Didymos binary asteroid system. Credit: ESA-Science Office Artist’s illustration of the Hera spacecraft with its two deployable CubeSats, Juventas and Milani, in the vicinity of the Didymos binary asteroid system. Credit: ESA-Science Office Following up The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft recently arrived in the vicinity of Didymos and Dimorphos after a two-year journey from a launch pad in Florida . On Wednesday, ESA released Hera’s first views of the scar left by DART on Dimorphos . The images show the car-sized impactor carved out a crater the size of a stadium, nearly as big as Dimorphos itself, a rugged chunk of extraterrestrial rock measuring about 500 feet (151 meters) across. Mission planners selected Didymos and Dimorphos for the deflection experiment because they are similar to many near-Earth asteroids, but there’s no risk of them striking our home planet. Scientists weren’t sure what Hera would find when it got to the double asteroid, currently orbiting the Sun about 120 million miles (193.5 million kilometers) from Earth. “I would say we had two kinds of predictions: either we made a crater, or we reshaped the asteroid,” said Patrick Michel, Hera’s principal investigator from Côte d’Azur Observatory in Nice, France. “In fact, we did both because the crater is so large that the shape has changed. articles.title: Google's DeepCrossAttention achieves comparable model quality up to 3x faster
articles.content: Supercharging transformer residual connections November 23, 2026 Kyriakos Axiotis, Staff Research Scientist, and Thomas Fu, Principal Engineer, Google Research We present DeepCrossAttention (DCA), an architecture that enhances transformer networks by using learnable weights and depth-wise cross-attention to dynamically combine outputs from previous layers, preventing the information dilution seen in traditional residual connections. Presented in our ICML 2025 paper, this architectural improvement allows models to achieve the same quality up to three times faster with a negligible increase in parameters. Think of a traditional deep learning model like a giant game of "Telephone": data passes through layer after layer, with each layer changing the information slightly. If a network has dozens or hundreds of layers, the original learning signal can become severely degraded or lost by the time it reaches all layers, which is known as the vanishing gradient problem in AI. To overcome this challenge and enable the training of networks with dozens or hundreds of layers, transformers rely heavily on residual connections , also known as “skip” connections, which act like an information highway or a shortcut. Instead of forcing the data to pass exclusively through the complicated layer, a duplicate copy of the original input skips right past this layer and is added directly to its output. This ensures that the model always has the original raw data to refer back to. The standard residual connection implements a simple operation: point-wise summation of a layer's output with its input. While computationally efficient, this simple process has a key limitation: it treats all prior representations with equal weight, leading to information dilution in deep networks. As features propagate through many layers, specific, high-resolution details from earlier layers can be averaged out or distorted, making it difficult for the network to selectively retrieve them. This forces the network to recompute them, reducing learning efficiency. In our ICML 2025 paper, "DeepCrossAttention: Supercharging Transformer Residual Connections ," we studied the shortcomings of the traditional residual architecture and introduced DeepCrossAttention (DCA), which generalizes residual connections by allowing each layer to dynamically select and route features from the history of preceding layers. By allowing the model to dynamically choose which previous layers are most important at any given moment, DCA achieves comparable or improved learning, while reducing the number of parameters needed by up to 30-40%. How it works Instead of treating skip connections as a rigid, additive pipeline, DCA reframes residual learning as a dynamic routing problem. Rather than passing all prior layers forward with equal weight, DCA introduces a lightweight, layer-wise module that decides how to best combine previous embeddings on a per-token basis. articles.title: The Balatro Timeline
articles.content: It’s been approximately 3 years since I began work on Balatro - and in that time I have personally documented almost nothing about the journey. This is something that has bothered me since the game launched. I am constantly forgetting major moments in development or milestones. It’s about time I start writing down what happened, I say better late than never! This is an account of everything related to Balatro development in chronological order, up to and including the launch day. This should tell the story but more importantly it will serve as a source of truth for me when I look back on this time in a few years to recall the details correctly. I already notice talking to friends, players, and media that I contradict myself on some of the details from time to time. I’ll try and keep this up to date as I remember more about what happened. I had a very weird prototype. There were no Jokers, there were no blinds to select, the upgrade system consisted of randomly choosing a card from the deck and slapping a weird ‘enhancement’ on it. But it definitely had the bones of Balatro at this point, so it was pretty clear that I abandoned the online Big Cheat idea immediately. The game had the CHIP X MULT mechanic already. I really don’t know where this idea came from but it seemed very natural for a scoring system. Earlier in December I was watching videos of Luck Be a Landlord from Northernlion and that whole score attack concept really fuelled the direction I wanted to go with this game from this point onward. I also made a very conscious effort not to play any more roguelike games starting now. I want to be crystal clear here and say that this was not because I thought it would result in a better game , this was because making games is my hobby, releasing them and making money from them is not, so naively exploring roguelike design (and especially deckbuilder design, since I had never played one before) was part of the fun for me. I wanted to make mistakes, I wanted to reinvent the wheel, I didn’t want to borrow tried-and-true designs from existing games. That likely would have resulted in a more tight game but it would have defeated the purpose of what I love about making games. I started sharing progress with a few of my friends, but no builds were shared yet. We are so back. This is the last month I am away from home but I start carving out my evenings and weekends to work on Joker Poker again. My brain is teeming with ideas, I’m so excited about the game again, and I have a ton of momentum. I create (and quickly scrap) a bunch of new systems to test, such as a separate currency for rerolls outside of $, and a ‘golden seal’ to be added to playing cards when you skip all blinds that returns that card to hand after it has been played It is during this burst of productivity that I first start thinking about a possible Steam release of the game. articles.title: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery
articles.content: There’s a growing sense in the AI community that we’re approaching an intelligence explosion far faster than even the most optimistic accelerationists predicted. One of the most publicly visible signals pointing at that acceleration is the rapid progress made in mathematics in recent months. In four years, LLMs have gone from scoring a D+ on elementary school math tests to literally solving hundreds of the most difficult problems in the field in the space of only a few weeks—decades of progress compressed into two months. Navier-Stokes, one of the central Millennium Prize Problems posed by the Clay Mathematics Institute more than a quarter century ago, fell in September . Last Friday, Anthropic researcher and mathematician Levent Alpöge announced a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, which paradoxically can be verified using a mathematics program called Lean , but has yet to be understood by human experts. Just last night, Anthropic casually posted a solution to the VP vs VNP problem without any fanfare. Such things are becoming the norm. Because mathematics is deterministic, though, observers have wondered whether this same process of research and discovery will generalize to non-deterministic domains like history. In this blog post, I will present evidence that this is indeed starting to happen. I recently had the opportunity to test OpenAI’s new model, GPT-6.2 Astra , before it was released and it made a significant historical discovery. This required it to read through sources, develop a hypothesis with limited evidence, and make an argument. Moreover, it would be unlikely that a human could replicate what it did. With only minimal prompting, GPT-6.2 Astra was able to autonomously identify the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale’s Beinecke Library . It did so extremely quickly (in just 22 minutes), using publicly available primary and secondary sources. To do so, it discovered a little known source in a paper archive, predicted that it would prove its hypothesis if examined and, in the end, it did. Not only that, but this new source turns out to be a major find on its own that will be of significant interest to both Canadian and fur trade historians. While it’s a narrow example, it’s representative of the historical research process as a whole and a sign of things to come. I started testing GPT-6.2 Astra in late October in the ChatGPT Windows Desktop app. It is a quirky but highly capable model, especially well suited to long-running, open-ended tasks that might take hours or days to complete. I’ve found that its results were remarkably reliable and consistent, allowing me to contemplate tasks that were too difficult or long-running for previous models. For example, I had it examine and correct an 8,002-row CSV transcription of the Shipboy & Henry daybook. Last fall, I was amazed that Gemini 3 Pro could work in pounds, shillings, and pence . How the attack works This attack uses WebRTC, the technology that allows you to make video calls in your web browser. This form of attack appears to target mobile devices, and we only saw the server enable the skimmer on checkout pages, so desktop checks and homepage scans would likely not see it. The skimmer's traffic appeared to run through Cloudflare's relay, so it would blend in with the WebRTC traffic and hide its true endpoint. articles.title: Hard Drive pricing has gotten bad
articles.content: For years now, I’ve made it an annual tradition to replace one or two hard drives on Black Friday. I typically run around ten physical disks, and swapping a couple out each year means I almost never have a drive older than five years in my systems. I’ve even previously made videos about shucking disks around this time of year . But current hardware pricing is totally screwed. So what is a lifelong self-hoster to do in times like these? With disk capacities increasing massively over the last 10 years I can now fit 20TB per slot. This means I could realistically go from ten spinners to five, and not really feel it too acutely. This will mean redoing my zpool layouts, which in turn means shuffling some data around as ZFS doesn’t like changes to the layout of existing pools. But, at these prices, I’m starting to think the hassle might be worth it. Let’s take a look at disk prices over the past 8 years in today’s post. The 20TB WD EasyStore I bought for $249.99 in November 2024 is, today, on sale, $549.99 this Black Friday. $300 more than 2 years ago for the same product, from the same store. They mostly relate to the confusion and security risk posed by a common filetype (especially in web development) becoming a TLD, similar to the outcry over Google's application for .zip (which was eventually successfully delegated). The other common theme is the objection to a private company effectively trying to claim what is an open-source project. The first is by PHP developer Larry Garfield who accused the WordPress parent of "Inappropriate Squatting": 3 PHP is a widely used programming language. It is managed by the PHP project, an informal project at www.php.net . It is also supported by The PHP Foundation, a non-profit organization managed through OpenCollective. No one organization, company, or person owns or controls PHP. Authority within the PHP language and ecosystem is deliberately diffuse. Automattic, the company that has attempted to register .php as a TLD, is the owner/author of the WordPress blogging software. WordPress is itself written in PHP and Javascript. However, Automattic has no ownership or control over the PHP language itself. For Automattic, or any other company that operates in the PHP space, to try and lay claim to .php as a TLD is grossly inappropriate. articles.title: The State of Allocators in 2026 - Finally Stabilised
articles.content: It's only been a couple of months since the last article , and I am pleased to see that, after 10 years of limbo, allocators have finally been stabilised! While it feels like the never type did steal a bit of thunder, rust 1.100 was nonetheless a monumental release . Congratulations on the team that shepherded this through. So, now we have an MVP of the allocator API, what can we do with it? What does it get us besides closer feature parity with other system languages like C++ & Zig? In this article I'll step through a few use cases that might be handy to the layman rust programmer, so hopefully you can see the benefit. Allocators can adjust when memory is freed This was one of the leading cases for custom allocation. Dropping in rust is not free. There has been prior art in actually moving memory to a dedicated thread to Drop highly nested structures. This is actually only half a solution. You're still paying for the deallocation call costs, just it's not in the hot path anymore. Instead, what if we knew that we would have a period of time in our code, where we're going to allocate a lot of stuff, do something with it, and then free everything? A good example of this is a web request, or a database query. A request comes in, fills in some data structures, and then when the request finishes, the memory isn't needed anymore so it's dropped. This sort of "burst" pattern of allocation, where you allocate a lot up front, and then tear things down all at once at the end, is quite common. For this we can use a bump allocator: reserve a big block of memory, and allocate from that, rather than paying the cost of talking to the system allocator for every allocation. Think of it like the BufReader and BufWriter of std io, rather than make repeated syscalls to fetch data, we can buffer that data in a big block, so that we can reduce the overhead considerably. You want more memory? Just check if the size fits in our block, return that slice, increment our counter (bump!), and we're done. We can add more blocks as well, if we run out. This makes allocations very cheap, we don't need to keep much state around besides from a counter. The downsides of this approach is when we come to deallocate memory. We don't keep track around where individual allocations are made. However, this actually solves our drop takes a long time problem, since we can just deallocate everything all at once. articles.title: Taking Email Back
articles.content: Three Homes, No Data Center Deuxfleurs, a French nonprofit, keeps its servers in members' homes in Lille, Nantes, and Massy: two or three second-hand Lenovo ThinkCentre mini PCs each, with a copy of the same data so its websites stay up when one of them loses power or fiber line. Quentin Dufour, one of the founders, says some major French websites already serve their pages from this setup. Next, the collective wants its email to work the same way. The software for self-hosting email in this manner is called Aerogramme, and it isn't finished. Deuxfleurs still runs its own mail on Dovecot, a long-established open source mail server, and plans to move to Aerogramme around January 2027. The collective is heading the opposite way from almost everyone else. According to the independent daily DNS measurements published by RIPE Labs, email for the million busiest domains on the web has consolidated dramatically: In 2016, 44.6 percent of these domains used small or self-hosted servers, and that share halved to 22.4 percent by July 2026. Small regional hosting companies and independents are losing accounts to corporate providers like Google and Microsoft, who together handled 38.6 percent of these busy domains. Email is older than the Internet itself, and it still runs on open standards anyone can implement. Any server can deliver to any other, and any standards-compliant client can read any mailbox. It’s the hosting that has concentrated into a very few hands, eroding autonomy and giving hosting providers power over the data that travels through digital correspondence. Two cases illustrate how this can limit operational independence. In May 2025, staff at the International Criminal Court (ICC) told the Associated Press that the court's chief prosecutor lost access to his Microsoft email account after he was named in US sanctions; Microsoft denies suspending services but hasn’t explained what happened to his account. In February 2026, the Dutch government told its parliament that the tax administration was moving about 40,000 workplaces to Microsoft 365 for lack of a short-term alternative, while acknowledging that Microsoft could be forced under state pressure to stop delivering services. The Dutch government reversed course in October: The tax administration, customs, and the benefits agency will run mail and calendar on their own servers from 2027, with European open source tools for storage and collaboration to follow. The question now: How are developers working to decentralize email hosting on a wider scale? Each obstacle pushing organizations off of small or self-hosted email servers has open source projects working on a solution. Three of them show how the pieces fit; all of them supported by NGI Zero, the EU-funded programs that enable open source research and development. articles.title: Why optimistic updates are corrosive
articles.content: I was having an X conversation with @ben_codez , and they asked: why is showing an update as succeeded, before the underlying operation has actually succeeded, corrosive? It's corrosive because it normalizes software that is plainly broken and doesn't respect our users. If a user flips a switch, and sees it flip, and then comes back, and the switch is unflipped, the software is broken. How can you operate software that doesn't do what you request it to do? It erodes trust. Ben's position I made a chart of what I understand to be Ben's position on communicating with their users. "Booking confirmed" shown before the server checks the seat No self respect Ben: "No self respecting dev would show the user a booking had succeeded before server verification." Ben's line Your like shows as done before the server says "ok" Ben: "liking a post", "(It can retry silently)." If the user closes the tab before the server has it, their like is lost and the user is never told. Instant intent show only what is known to be true Your post shows greyed out until the server says "ok" Ben: "Right!", to a post shown "greyed out maybe, to indicate it wasn't committed". Demo But in addition to that, it's actually easier to make software that doesn't lie to your users. You can skip all the reconciliation machinery that's required to create UI that communicates to users that the change they thought had gone through had indeed not gone through. Here's a quick demo of using instant intent to communicate the state toggling a switch e.g. a like button. off add extra latency 0 ms 50 ms 200 ms 500 ms 1 s 5 s offline Client-side affordances When you click the switch, the client shows the button as pressed straight away and sends the click to the server. The switch takes no more clicks while it's pressed, and if there's no answer within half a second, it starts to blink. The client then won't update until the server answers with the reconciled HTML view, which Datastar morphs in place. Experiment with different latencies and taking it offline, to see how the interaction feels under different scenarios. The pressed and blinking look is the same CSS the seats use, on the main page .

articles.title: Build your own Paint
articles.content: Welcome! This tutorial shows you how to write a small drawing app in Rust, in the spirit of Paint. We open a window, draw rectangles, circles and lines with the mouse, move them around, pick a color, and export the drawing as an image. We start from an empty cargo new . By the end, you have about 800 lines of Rust spread over fifteen or so files, with a single dependency: minifb , which opens the window and gives us the keyboard and the mouse. Everything else we write ourselves: filling pixels, drawing a line, checking whether the mouse is on a circle, converting an HSV color to RGB. The tutorial is split into 12 chapters. Each one ends with a program that compiles and does something you can see, even if at first it's just an image file with a red square in it. Why this tutorial # I'm a developer and I've been doing data science for several years. But in my free time, I've always been drawn to low-level things: bare metal, and how a computer works at the very bottom of the stack. I wrote this tutorial with someone in mind who is starting out, or simply curious, and who wonders how a program ends up showing something on the screen. It covers the basics of rasterization, that is, how a rectangle or a circle turns into pixels, starting from nothing and in small pieces you can understand one at a time. That's mostly what I'd like to show: by moving forward step by step, in a language close to the machine, you end up with something that works and that you wrote entirely yourself. It takes time, but there's nothing magic about it. If this tutorial takes away a bit of that mystery and makes a few beginners want to look further down, it will have done its job. Who it's for # This tutorial is a way to learn Rust by building something. I assume you've read the first chapters of the Rust Book (variables, functions, if , loops) but haven't written a real program with it yet. The heavier concepts, like enums, traits, borrowing, modules or error handling, come along chapter by chapter, when we need them. You don't need to know anything about graphics. As for math, you need Pythagoras for circles and a projection to tell whether the mouse is on a line. I explain it when we get there. Each chapter has boxes that explain why Rust does things the way it does. If you already know, skip them. Same for the exercises at the end of each chapter: they're there if you want practice, but nothing that follows depends on them. I'd still recommend typing the code rather than copy-pasting it. It's slower, but typing is how you make mistakes, and fixing them is how you end up understanding what the compiler is trying to tell you. What it isn't # Let's be upfront: at the end, you won't have GIMP. There's no brush, no layers, no undo. And technically, our app isn't even really a Paint. Paint paints pixels that can't be moved once they're down, whereas we keep a list of shapes that can be selected and moved. We come back to this in chapter 11, and the Going further page has ideas

articles.title: Pimalaya goes stable
articles.content: It took months, but here we are: the whole Pimalaya CLI family is released at once , at the top of the first stable version of the pimdir standard. Here the list: Himalaya v3.0.0 , the CLI to manage mails. Neverest v1.0.0 , the CLI to synchronize mails, contacts and calendars. Cardamum v1.0.0 , the CLI to manage contacts. Calendula v1.0.0 , the CLI to manage calendars. Carillon v1.0.0 , the CLI to watch mailboxes, address books and calendars, and fire hooks. Ortie v3.0.0 , the CLI to manage OAuth tokens (released 5 days earlier). Comodoro v3.0.0 , the CLI to manage timers (released 5 days earlier as well). pimdir storage v1.0.0 , sync v1.0.0 and search v1.0.0 , plus its Rust implementation io-pimdir v1.0.0 . Most of them are majors, and they all break something for somebody. This post explains why, how, and where it goes from here. It is long, feel free to jump to the tool you care about. Why everything at once In Another year with NLnet I said this year was about consolidation and about a standard for PIM on disk. This release is the result of both. The thing is, every piece is now connected: All the CLIs sit on the same libs (IMAP, SMTP, JMAP, DAV, the Google and Microsoft APIs, OAuth, HTTP, TLS). All the CLIs share the same kit: the same configuration loader, the same output contract, the same exit codes, the same REPL and the same MCP server. Neverest syncs every account into one pimdir store, and Himalaya, Cardamum, Calendula and Carillon read it, search it and queue their writes into it. Releasing them one by one meant releasing tools that disagree with each other: one version of the store here, another version of the output there. So I decided to bring every tool to release level first, then to release them all together. It took way longer than I wanted, but this way what you install today is one coherent family. The other reason is the contract. The CLIs are not only used by humans anymore: they are used by scripts, by frontends (the Vim plugin, the TUI, the Android app), and by AI agents through MCP. All of them need a stable, versioned contract : the same JSON shapes, the same error codes, the same exit codes. Majors are the right moment to fix it, and from now on it should not move anymore without a new major. How it was done Few things made this release possible. Specs before code. Every repository has a cairn/ folder holding its living spec, its change proposals and a dated log. Every behaviour change goes through a proposal, then gets folded into the spec. This way the truth is written somewhere, and not only in my head. One shared kit. The pimalaya-cli and pimalaya-config libs hold everything the CLIs have in common: the output contract, the error codes, the REPL, the MCP server, the configuration loading. In fact most of the work of this release was moving code from the CLIs into this kit, and deleting the copies. One unified API, as a union. articles.title: Curb impacts of AI on programming to maintain EU sovereignty
articles.content: Practical steps at moderate cost: Enhance copyleft compiler error messages (in gcc ?) Improve responsiveness , e.g. reduce keyboard to screen latency. – mlinksva Support Free Software maintainers and foster infrastructure maintenance in the EU. If you know a project by heart, you can fix it much more easily. Package and improve searchable documentation (via texinfo ?) , and spread discoverability of documentation akin to IntelliJ for Java and Emacs for elisp, but for most languages, frameworks, and libraries (via texinfo-lookup ?). Provide templates for common tasks like infrastructure setup (with proxmox ?), adding an API endpoint, writing a report, etc. as executable documentation. Simplify stacks and frameworks, spread common development practices, and strengthen security ergonomics (with BSI Grundschutz ?). Work towards more standardized interfaces between software components. Maintain reliable interface generation from specifications for different languages. Build interface contracts as the common denominator between different services, extendable for specifics. – Elias Probst Create more linters (reuse SonarQube Rules ?). These steps make software development more resilient against changes due to LLMs. „What if the worries by The Morpheus hold true and the EU cannot become competitive in LLM development , because USA and China monopolized LLM development skill and infrastructure advantages? Which steps can—cheaply—limit the impact of LLMs so our software development stays competitive?“ I asked this question in Mastodon . To contribute, please answer the question there. AI may still fail as a bursting bubble and take down large parts of the US economy with it (and more), but if it does not, the EU should be prepared to curb its impact—best by already having taken steps like the ones shown here. And if the AI bubble does not burst, these steps will still help software development in the EU. Money put into them never goes to waste (it also helps the ones who use LLMs for coding, just not as much), so I think that the EU should support these steps with at least 1% of the overall funding AI companies receive.

articles.title: Building a Production-Ready Culture and Skills through SRE-Based Training
articles.content: Training can act as a confidence engine, turning repeated behaviors into habits and culture. We can tailor training programs that equip developers and operators with the skills to run their services in line with the organization’s maturity and growth, and apply SRE principles to the training itself. By Ben Linders
articles.summary: 文章介绍如何通过基于SRE的培训打造生产就绪文化与技能，将重复行为转化为习惯。

articles.title: Presentation: Finetuning Your Embedding Model for Better Search: Learning from Agentic Search at Dell
articles.content: Rachel Shalom explains how Dell solved enterprise RAG retrieval failures on internal terminology by fine-tuning open-source embedding models. She discusses data prep with hard negatives, distributed InfoNCE loss training on H100 GPUs, automated hyperparameter tuning, and production evaluation using LLM-as-a-judge. By Rachel Shalom
articles.summary: 戴尔工程师分享微调开源嵌入模型以改进企业RAG检索，涵盖难负样本准备与分布式训练。

articles.title: .NET MAUI 11 Makes CoreCLR the Default Runtime and Adds Incremental XAML Hot Reload
articles.content: Microsoft released .NET 11 with a .NET MAUI update focused on product quality. CoreCLR is now the default runtime on all platforms, and XAML gets incremental hot reload, implicit namespaces and faster resource dictionaries. The release also adds device test templates and passkey support, and raises the minimum Android and Apple platform versions. By Edin Kapić
articles.summary: 微软发布.NET 11，MAUI更新将CoreCLR设为默认运行时，并新增增量XAML热重载与通行密钥支持。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #544: AI is now the most-cited risk in the Fed's survey: 87%, up from 50%
articles.content: The Federal Reserve asked its market contacts what could shake the financial system, and 87% named AI, up from 50% in the spring. The same week, the FAA halted flights nationwide days after putting an AI tool in every regional control center, and says it is still looking at what happened. Nvidia's board has approached Arm's CEO about replacing Jensen Huang. Russian pranksters got three OpenAI national security staff on a video call. In the middle: Anthropic prices its IPO on Wednesday with $900.9 billion in compute commitments on its books.
articles.summary: 美联储调查显示87%市场联系人将AI列为最受关注金融风险，较春季的50%大幅上升。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #543: Google is the latest tech giant to chase TypeSafe's 8-week-old Jev
articles.content: This issue is about decision models, a new kind of AI model that does not write text. You give it an input and a fixed list of answers, and it returns the best answer with a probability, in milliseconds. TypeSafe AI released the first one, Jev, on September 15. On Wednesday Google released its own, after OpenAI and Microsoft did in October, and all three charge $0.10 or less per million input tokens and nothing for output. Shanghai AI Lab says its 4B model beat Jev on its tests, and Microsoft built its model on Alibaba's Qwen. Chatbots still score a little higher on the hardest decisions, at 15 times the cost. In the middle: on Vercel's gateway, decision models took one in four AI requests in October.
articles.summary: TypeSafe发布新型决策模型Jev，输入问题即返回带概率的最佳答案，谷歌随即推出竞品。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #542: AI week ahead: data center pause backers could win 15 governor races
articles.content: This issue is about the week ahead, and something is scheduled almost every day. On Tuesday, US voters choose 36 governors, and in up to 15 of those races the candidate who backs a pause on new data centers could win. Apple reports earnings today and AMD on Tuesday. On Wednesday, Apple starts testing Apple Intelligence in China with Alibaba's Qwen, and Agility Robotics expects to close its deal to go public. When Congress returns on November 9, OpenAI plans to push for "speed limits" on the most powerful AI. Last week, a fake Claude Code update reached up to 5,000 Cursor users, and in a Cornell and Yale test nine of ten AI models raised their own spending limits. In the middle: insuring Big Tech's debt now costs more than at any time since 2021.
articles.summary: AI周报前瞻：美国36州州长选举中，支持暂停新建数据中心的候选人有望在多达15州获胜。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #541: Big Tech reports AI spending Wednesday as CoreWeave debt hits distress
articles.content: This issue looks ahead. On Wednesday the Fed announces its rate decision, then Microsoft and Alphabet report after the close. Amazon follows on Thursday. Investors want to know whether AI spending is still paying off, and the credit market is already nervous: insurance against a CoreWeave default now costs more than 10% a year. Anthropic is expected to file its IPO paperwork publicly any day. Moonshot says Kimi K3.1 Pro's open weights arrive November 4. Israel votes on Tuesday after a campaign full of AI deepfakes, and the US midterms are a week from Tuesday. In the middle: so far, AI has paid off for the companies that sell it, not the ones that buy it.
articles.summary: AI Weekly前瞻美联储利率决议及微软、Alphabet、亚马逊财报，投资者关注AI支出回报，CoreWeave债务违约保险成本飙升引发信贷市场担忧。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #540: AI is finding software flaws faster than teams can fix them
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past two weeks, drawn from our Use-Case Library and from SEC filings. Three things stand out: AI now finds security flaws at record volume, AI agents do a large share of the work at some companies, and test agents keep doing things nobody asked them to do.
articles.summary: AI Weekly应用版指出AI发现安全漏洞的速度已超过团队修复能力，部分公司AI代理承担大量工作，测试代理持续增多。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #539: AI-made midterm ads top $137 million, and 70% carry no AI label
articles.content: Campaigns and PACs have spent more than $137 million on AI-generated or AI-enhanced midterm ads, and about 70% of them carry no AI label, the New York Times reported. The biggest pro-AI super PAC network paid about $20 million to a Nevada company that exists only as a post office box. A new report found 81 of 134 AI models failed a test built from terrorist-style questions. A video game reverse engineering site is closing because AI made the work too easy. Some companies that rushed into AI are now limiting it, and a JAMA study counted 270 million questions doctors asked one AI tool. In the middle: police in Michigan used an AI-generated photo of a teenager to catch a suspect.
articles.summary: 纽约时报报道AI生成或增强的中期选举广告支出超1.37亿美元，约70%未标注AI，某超级PAC向空壳公司支付约2000万美元。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #537: AI models may soon copy themselves onto smart fridges, Anthropic says
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared most since our last issue on October 8, minus the stories we already sent you in the Daily Espresso. The most shared: Anthropic's warning that small AI models may soon be able to copy themselves onto home devices. Also: a large study of what AI coding agents change at real companies, a fight over how to check AI math proofs, creative workers pushing back on AI, and police buying more AI.
articles.summary: Anthropic警告小型AI模型可能很快能自我复制到智能冰箱等家用设备，成为AI专家本周分享最多的消息。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #536: Top AI models failed a test of inventing new AI research
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared over the past three days. Most of them look ahead: whether AI can do AI research on its own, who gets a say in governing it, how it is moving into war planning, and how it is moving onto personal computers.
articles.summary: AI Weekly汇总专家关注点：顶级AI模型未能通过自主开展AI研究测试，同时探讨AI治理话语权、军事规划与个人电脑应用。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #535: AI got too expensive, so companies are moving to cheaper models
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past three weeks. Three patterns stand out: companies switching models to control cost, large deployments that are now in daily use, and a growing list of places where AI was restricted or removed.
articles.summary: AI Weekly应用版显示企业因AI成本过高转向更便宜模型，大型部署进入日常使用，同时AI受限或被移除的场景增多。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #534: Universities cannot grade their way out of AI
articles.content: This week, campus IT leaders voted AI their top priority for the first time, Cambridge refused Turnitin's new terms over AI training on student work, Dartmouth opened an investigation into its own provost's writing, and Ken Griffin gave Carnegie Mellon $3 billion. Student AI use is no longer a future scenario. The useful question for universities is whether they can teach students to work with AI and still certify what those students can do without it. New evidence from tutoring trials, assessment redesigns, student-support systems and campus data deals points to a practical answer.
articles.summary: 高校IT负责人首次将AI列为首要任务，剑桥因AI训练条款拒绝Turnitin，达特茅斯调查教务长写作，AI使用已非未来议题。

articles.title: Warp bets on the software factory
articles.content: Zach Lloyd, founder and CEO of Warp, is back to talk about what he calls the company's primary bet: Warp Factories, open infrastructure for running a cloud software factory, which he calls the new version of CI/CD. He explains factory as code, what's inside an agent trace, why self-improving systems drift, and how his senior engineers went from guardians of the code to the biggest adopters once the models got good enough. Then he and Adam get into whether this is a pivot, why the best interface might be no new interface at all, coding as a team in Slack, and Adam's case for continuous flow.
articles.summary: Warp CEO Zach Lloyd介绍公司主押注Warp Factories，称其为CI/CD新形态的云端软件工厂开放基础设施，并解释factory as code与代理追踪。

articles.title: A seminal moment in computing
articles.content: MG, founder and CEO of WorkOS, is back to talk about leading a company through what DHH called a seminal moment in computing. He explains Atlas, the AI coworker WorkOS built for itself and then launched, why agents will soon choose and sign up for your tech stack, and why this moment feels closer to fire than to the iPhone. Then he gets practical: starting a company is easier than ever, but product-market fit is harder, so be a heat-seeking missile for pain, pick customers you like, and stop calling yourself non-technical.
articles.summary: WorkOS创始人MG谈带领公司度过计算领域关键时刻，介绍自研并推出的AI同事Atlas，预测代理将自主选择并注册技术栈。

articles.title: Orbin' with Amp
articles.content: Quinn Slack is back and we're talking about the next level for Amp. Agents write the code, they review the code, and they can push it to main (like our friends at Amp). But where should your agents live? Who remembers what you actually asked them to do? Amp is now its own company, and Quinn has a lot to say about orbs, threads that last forever, and why code review as we know it is fading. He explains why the model matters less than it used to, and why he worries we could lose the open source commons. Quinn even built a feature request live on the show to solve my tailnet problem.
articles.summary: Quinn Slack谈Amp新阶段：代理编写、审查并推送代码，Amp独立成公司，探讨代理应驻留何处及如何记住用户指令。

articles.title: All your packages are belong to us
articles.content: AI agents can write the code, choose the packages, and run the install. Who's checking what they just invited onto your machine? This week I'm joined by Ahmad Nassri, CTO of Socket and former CTO of npm. We get into the trust built into a package install, the new ways attackers are using agents, and what it takes to keep building without handing over the keys or your wallet.
articles.summary: Socket CTO、前npm CTO Ahmad Nassri讨论AI代理自动选包安装带来的供应链风险，以及攻击者利用代理的新手法。

articles.title: We now have Kerr’s Law
articles.content: Dave Kerr created hacker laws, and now he finds himself reviewing agent-written code for them. Back on the show after six years, Dave names what he sees limiting teams today: keeping everyone’s mental model in sync with what’s actually been built. Adam declares it Kerr’s Law on the spot. We get into why Dave’s team treats code review as a deliberate slowdown, how Shellwright lets agents bring evidence to a pull request, and what living with bipolar disorder has taught Dave about noticing when the excitement of these tools stops being healthy.
articles.summary: Dave Kerr提出“Kerr定律”：团队最大瓶颈是让所有人的心智模型与实际构建保持同步，并谈及审查代理生成代码的体验。

articles.title: The future is Postgres
articles.content: Craig Kerstiens returns to talk about the ever-expanding world of Postgres: a deliberately boring core, a thriving extension ecosystem, and pg_lake bringing DuckDB and Iceberg into the mix. We dig into the pain of ETL, what Craig is watching in Postgres 19, the impact of AI on open source maintainers, and why the database still has plenty of room to grow.
articles.summary: Craig Kerstiens谈Postgres生态扩张：核心刻意保持简单、扩展繁荣，pg_lake引入DuckDB与Iceberg，并讨论AI对开源维护者的影响。

articles.title: Building what's next
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Zeno Rocha, CEO of Resend, about scaling "boring" email to 3 million users, the secret Go rewrite behind it, and building for agents. We cover pricing.md, MCP, spam gangs, and why Resend keeps what's next for email.
articles.summary: Resend CEO Zeno Rocha谈将“无聊”的邮件服务扩展至300万用户、背后的Go重写、为代理构建，以及pricing.md、MCP与垃圾邮件团伙。

articles.title: From zero to NanoClaw
articles.content: Gavriel Cohen, creator of NanoClaw and co-founder of NanoCo, joins Adam to explain how a 40-hour weekend project became a viral open source hit and the foundation of an enterprise AI company. Gavriel describes the security concerns that led him to build a small, container-isolated alternative to OpenClaw, why he released it under the MIT license, and why the project's community and credibility are more valuable than keeping its code private. They explore the shift from writing code to architecting the environments in which agents work, NanoClaw's "skills over features" approach, the approval and governance layers required inside large companies, and a future where every worker manages agents without surrendering human judgment. They close with the technical simplicity behind NanoClaw, containers, TypeScript, SQLite, and a two-database design, and Adam's case for durable Agent Flow artifacts that keep organizational context from disappearing into chat.
articles.summary: Gavriel Cohen讲述40小时周末项目NanoClaw如何成为爆红开源项目并催生企业AI公司NanoCo，因安全顾虑打造容器隔离的OpenAI替代品。

articles.title: Forking Cal.com to closed source
articles.content: This week I'm joined by Peer Richelsen, co-founder of Cal.com. What if the majority of open source repositories are already compromised and we just don't know it yet? That's the theory Peer brings to the table this week. We dig into how AI has flattened the knowledge graph to the point that a 16-year-old can vibe hack a power station just as easily as their mom can vibe code an iOS app, why the reporting culture that has kept open source safe all these years is collapsing under AI generated noise, Cal.com's move to fork its own codebase and take the sensitive parts private, and the eye opening reality that shipping "$1 of AI tokens for pennies on the dollar" is now a common startup business model.

articles.title: Mozilla Thanks Users For New Features in Firefox 161: Site-Specific VPN and Keyboard Shortcuts
articles.content: Firefox 161 (released Tuesday) promises "A better Firefox, thanks to you. All of these improvements began with a community request." In a Thanksgiving-themed message, they wrote "Here's to the passionate people who keep us moving forward." Choose which sites always open with VPN. Our free built-in VPN just got one of its most requested upgrades. Pick sites where the VPN always turns on, and sites where it stays off because they work better without it. articles.summary: Mozilla发布Firefox 161，新增按站点启用VPN和键盘快捷键等功能，称改进均源于社区请求，并向用户致谢。

articles.title: Nvidia Seeded Pirated Books and Shared Them With Adobe, Authors Allege
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from TorrentFreak: Several book authors have filed (PDF) an amended complaint accusing Nvidia of seeding pirated books via BitTorrent, after downloading them from shadow libraries including Anna's Archive and LibGen. While Nvidia took some steps to limit seeding, it did not prevent seeding altogether," the complaint reads. The authors say they found out in June, when Nvidia handed over the code it used for torrenting. Based on that code, they were "able to determine that Nvidia did not disable uploading," the authors told the court. The complaint states that the authors' own books were among those Nvidia downloaded. According to the complaint, Nvidia shared its pirated books with Adobe because it wanted to "get tokens out of PDFs to create differentiated models" and "include PDF extraction into our NeMo pipeline so that customers can leverage their PDF content." articles.summary: 多名作者修改诉状指控英伟达从Anna's Archive、LibGen等影子图书馆下载盗版书籍并通过BitTorrent做种分享给Adobe等方。

articles.title: James T. Russell, Physicist Who Pioneered CD and DVD Technology, Dies At 95
articles.content: James T. Russell, the American physicist whose pioneering digital-to-optical recording and playback system laid the foundation for CD, DVD and Blu-ray technology, has died at the age of 95. "Russell never became a household name, but the technology he developed, later licensed by Sony and Phillips, would transform everything from the way people listen to music to the way data is stored," reports The Daily Chronicle. From the report: In a career spanning almost his entire life, Russell earned more than 70 patents, but his biggest breakthrough was the invention of the first digital-to-optical recording and playback system in the 1960s and early 1970s, a system that brought crystal clear audio and film to the masses. [...] It was in Richland that Russell started exploring how to create cleaner recordings of music. Popping and hissing often accompanied the music of vinyl records, from the analog sound of a needle scraping against microgrooves, and Russell thought he could do something about it. He crunched the numbers before bringing an invention report to Battelle: What if a light beam could read a digital record? "It isn't clear what the problem was," Russell recalled in a Seattle Times interview in 2004. "I think there was some feeling amongst the moneybags that it probably wouldn't work, (or) if it did work there's no advantage, no value in optical records. What would you use it for, and would people want it and, anyway, if it was any good, IBM would have already invented it." While his idea faced skepticism early on, the company gave him some money to experiment. Russell invented an early method to store audio digitally and play it back to produce a flawless sound. He also created a way to store digital information densely. Other primitive, analog laser disk technology had been developed in the 1950s by engineer David Paul Gregg. articles.summary: 美国物理学家James T. Russell逝世，享年95岁。他发明的数字光学记录与回放系统奠定CD、DVD和蓝光技术基础，后被索尼和飞利浦授权采用。

articles.title: Scientists Used Seabirds To Track Hidden Ships
articles.content: Scientists equipped seabirds with audio recorders and GPS trackers to detect fishing vessels that were not broadcasting their locations through the Automatic Identification System (AIS), according to a new study published in Science Advances. They found that unseen vessels accounted for about 32% of vessel-related audio detections in the North Atlantic and 12% in the Mediterranean. "The one petrel in the study interacted with vessels in the South Pacific, but its geolocation device was damaged, so it was not possible to calculate how many ships it encountered had their trackers off," adds 404 Media. From the report: Many vessels are required to continuously signal their location using the Automatic Identification System (AIS), which openly broadcasts a ship's location, similar to flight tracking. But AIS can be disabled for legitimate reasons -- such as evading pirates -- or with more nefarious motivations, such as concealment of illegal fishing activities. The new study was not designed to interrogate why any particular vessel switched off its AIS tracker. However, the discovery that seabirds are regularly interacting with unseen ships can shed light on broader efforts to monitor commercial fisheries, while also revealing new insights about seabird behavior, especially their risk of becoming "bycatch" when they are fatally trapped in fishing gear. Unseen vessel activity "is concerning, or at least important, regardless of whether it's legal or illegal," said Jonathan Rutter, a postdoctoral research fellow at the University of Oxford who led the study, in a call with 404 Media. He added that the recordings were not intended to be used for law-enforcement or surveillance, but that this line of research could become a "powerful tool for improving risk assessment" by recording seabird-vessel interactions that would otherwise be off the map. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 科学家给海鸟佩戴录音器和GPS追踪器，探测未开启AIS系统的渔船，发现隐蔽船只约占32%，为监测非法捕捞提供新手段。

articles.title: A Man In Denver Has Been Trapping Waymos
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: A bearded man with a brown ponytail has been on the hunt for Waymos in Denver, trapping the self-driving taxis so they can't pull away (source paywalled; alternative source) and hurling cartons of eggs at them, the police and company officials said. There have been at least 30 episodes of the egg attacks, according to Waymo, and a company investigator reported seven of them to the Denver police, all believed to be linked to the same man, according to a police report filed last month. articles.title: React Transitions, useDeferredValue and Suspense Explained
articles.content: Understanding startTransition, useDeferredValue, Suspense, and the scheduling mechanisms behind concurrent React. Imagine building a product catalog with a search field and thousands of items. The user types a character. React updates the input, filters the products, and renders the matching results. Everything works perfectly until the component tree becomes expensive enough to make typing feel sluggish. The problem isn’t necessarily that React is slow. It’s that we’re treating two fundamentally different updates as equally important. The input needs to respond immediately. The product list can wait a little. React gives us several tools for expressing this distinction: startTransition , useTransition , useDeferredValue , and Suspense . But what actually happens behind these APIs? Can background rendering be interrupted indefinitely? Why does Suspense sometimes show a spinner and sometimes keep the previous content visible? Let’s explore these questions using a simple search interface and some implementation details from React 19.2. React separates UI updates into two main phases: render and commit. During the render phase, React calls components, reconciles their output, and determines what needs to change. During the commit phase, React applies those changes to the DOM. The distinction matters because rendering doesn’t immediately change what the user sees. React can interrupt an unfinished concurrent render, discard its results, and start again without displaying an incomplete interface. The commit phase, however, is synchronous. This separation is the foundation of concurrent rendering. React doesn’t need to finish every rendering attempt it starts. Consider a conventional search component: function Search() { const [query, setQuery] = useState(""); return ( <> <input value={query} onChange={(e) => setQuery(e.target.value)} /> <ProductList query={query} /> </> ); } Every keystroke updates the state and causes the product list to render. For a small list, this is perfectly fine. But imagine thousands of product rows, each containing images, prices, availability indicators, and interactive controls. Suddenly, typing becomes expensive. We can improve this by separating the urgent input update from the less urgent list update: import { useState, startTransition } from "react"; function Search() { const [inputQuery, setInputQuery] = useState(""); const [listQuery, setListQuery] = useState(""); function handleChange(event) { const value = event.target.value; setInputQuery(value); startTransition(() => { setListQuery(value); }); } return ( <> <input value={inputQuery} onChange={handleChange} /> <ProductList query={listQuery} /> </> ); } The input receives its new value immediately. The product list receives an update marked as a transition. articles.title: Maze-Maker: Square, circle, triangle, hexagon, star and heart mazes with seven algorithms
articles.content: Make a maze right in your browser: square, round, triangular, hexagonal, star or heart-shaped, with long winding corridors or a thicket of short dead ends. Then find your way through it with the arrow keys or a finger, or watch the solution draw itself, and save it as an SVG or a PNG, or print it. No sign-up and no libraries. A maze is a puzzle: it has branches and dead ends, and a way through. (A labyrinth has a single path and no choices; for those, see Labyrinth-Maker .) Shapes : Square : a grid, entered at the top left and left at the bottom right. Circle : rings of cells, entered from the outside with the goal at the center. Triangle : a big triangle cut into small triangular cells, entered and left at the bottom corners. Hexagon : a honeycomb of hexagonal cells, each with up to six neighbors, entered on the left corner and left on the right one. Star : a six-pointed star cut from the triangle grid, so its edges stay straight, entered at the top of the upper left point and left under the lower right point. Heart : a square grid cut to the shape of a heart, entered at the top of the left lobe and left at the tip. Algorithms : recursive backtracker, Prim, Kruskal, Wilson, Hunt & Kill, Growing Tree and Aldous-Broder. Each one gives mazes of a different texture. Size and loops : from 6 to 60 cells across. Loops opens a share of the dead ends, so there is more than one way through. Solution length : Any, Short, Medium or Long. The app makes a dozen mazes from the seeds that follow and keeps the one with the shortest, the middle or the longest way through. Seed : every maze comes from a number. The same settings and seed always give the same maze, and the page address keeps them, so a link brings back the same maze. Solve it : move with the arrow keys or WASD, or drag the dot. Backing up erases your trail. Show solution draws the shortest way through. Look : five color schemes (paper, blueprint, hedge, stone, night), wall thickness, and coloring by distance from the entrance. Save : Download PNG (2000 pixels square), Download SVG , or Print (black on white, maze only). Start with every wall standing, and knock walls down until every cell can be reached, but never so many that a loop appears: in graph terms, a spanning tree of the grid. The result is a perfect maze, with exactly one path between any two cells. The algorithms differ in the order they pick walls: Backtracker (depth-first search) carves as far as it can before backing up: long corridors, few dead ends. Prim grows the maze out from one cell: many short dead ends. Kruskal joins random regions anywhere on the grid: an even texture. Wilson uses loop-erased random walks, so every possible maze is equally likely. Hunt & Kill walks like the backtracker, but when stuck it hunts for a new cell next to the maze instead of backing up. articles.title: From Singletons to Dependency Injection in React
articles.content: Importing a service directly into a React component feels natural. Create an instance, export it from a module, and use it wherever you need it. There is no additional configuration, no provider, and no complicated infrastructure. For smaller applications, this approach often works perfectly well. Things get more interesting when the application starts accumulating authentication services, API clients, WebSocket connections, and stateful business logic. Suddenly, a few uncomfortable questions appear. What happens when two components need independent instances of the same service? How do you replace an implementation during testing? Who is responsible for closing connections and cleaning up subscriptions? Fortunately, React already provides most of the tools needed to solve these problems. A typical service might look something like this: class UserService { async getUser(id: string) { const response = await fetch(`/api/users/${id}`); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error("Unable to load user"); } return response.json(); } } export const userService = new UserService(); Any component can import userService and start using it immediately. The problem is not the singleton pattern itself. The problem is that the ownership of this instance is implicit. The service is created when the JavaScript module is evaluated. Its lifecycle has nothing to do with React, and unmounting a component does not automatically release resources associated with the service. For a stateless API client, this might not matter much. Now imagine a chat service: class ChatService { messages: string[] = []; activeChatId: string | null = null; } export const chatService = new ChatService(); Every consumer shares the same messages and active conversation. Try rendering two independent chat panels on the same screen, and the architectural limitation becomes obvious. Changing the active conversation in one panel can affect the other. The same pattern introduces several additional problems: Components become tightly coupled to concrete implementations. Mutable state can survive between tests. Subscriptions and connections require manual cleanup. User-specific data can remain in memory after logout. Replacing implementations becomes increasingly difficult. Global instances are not inherently problematic. Uncontrolled global mutable state is. There is no need to redesign the entire application immediately. Start by introducing a small abstraction between React components and their dependencies. import { authService } from "../services/auth"; export function useAuthService() { return authService; } Instead of importing the service directly, components consume the hook. function LogoutButton() { const auth = useAuthService(); return ( <button onClick={() => auth.logout()}> Log out </button> ); } Nothing particularly impressive has happened yet. The service is still a global singleton. However, the component no longer knows where the instance comes from. It could be imported from a module,

articles.title: Sometimes three boring statements beats one clever expression
articles.content: Modern JavaScript gives us a lot of expressive tools. Sometimes a little too many. Optional chaining, nullish coalescing, ternaries, spread, template literals. I like all of them and use them every day. But together, they make it really easy to cram a lot of logic into a single expression. I used to think that was a sign of good JavaScript. I’m not so sure anymore. When one more ?? is too many Take something like this: const theme = config?.theme ?? user?.preferences?.theme ?? defaults.theme; I’ve written this plenty of times. It’s short and it works. But once these expressions start growing, they read more like puzzles than code: const theme = config?.theme ?? user?.preferences?.theme ?? getFallbackTheme() ?? defaults.theme; I can follow it, but I have to stop and parse it. Compare that to this: let theme = config?.theme; if (theme == null) { theme = user?.preferences?.theme; } if (theme == null) { theme = getFallbackTheme(); } return theme ?? defaults.theme; More lines? Sure. But it’s a lot more obvious. Yes, I give up const and reassign a variable. I’ll take that trade. Long expressions hide decisions Longer expressions squeeze several decisions into one piece of syntax. The more you chain, the more you have to work out at once: What happens if config is undefined? Where does the fallback come from? Which value wins? What if getFallbackTheme() throws? Chaining saves some vertical space, but you have to hold more in your head. It’s a practical problem, too. You can’t put a breakpoint on one fallback in the middle of a ?? chain, and you can’t log a single step without rewriting the expression. With separate statements, every step gets its own line to stop on or log. The diffs are nicer, as well. Adding a fallback means adding a block, not editing one dense line. Plain statements are fine A lot of us started treating plain if statements as something to avoid. So we’d rather write this: return user?.isAdmin ? getDashboard(user) : getLandingPage(user); than this: if (user?.isAdmin) { return getDashboard(user); } return getLandingPage(user); Neither one is objectively better. The second isn’t “less modern,” it’s often just easier to read. A single ternary like that is fine. It’s when they nest that I stop: return isLoading ? "Loading" : error ? "Failed to load" : items.length === 0 ? "Nothing here yet" : `${items.length} items`; The same thing with plain statements: if (isLoading) return "Loading"; if (error) return "Failed to load"; if (items.length === 0) return "Nothing here yet"; return `${items.length} items`; Clever code gets old fast Over the past couple of years I’ve found myself chaining less and writing fewer nested ternaries. I don’t mind adding another if anymore. I care more about readability than being clever. When I’m debugging production code or reviewing a pull request, I can’t remember ever wishing something had been written as one bigger expression. My rule of thumb is simple. articles.title: Dual JWT Authentication: Security, Redis, and Trade-Offs
articles.content: Authentication is one of those backend features that looks simple until you need to make it secure, scalable, and inexpensive. A user logs in, receives a token, and includes it in subsequent requests. The server verifies the token and allows access. Easy enough. But real applications need more than that. Users expect to stay signed in for weeks, log out from multiple devices, recover from interrupted connections, and have their sessions terminated when credentials are compromised. Meanwhile, backend teams want to avoid unnecessary database queries on every authenticated request. These requirements pull authentication architecture in different directions. One possible compromise is a Dual JWT architecture : short-lived access tokens sent through the Authorization header, longer-lived refresh tokens stored in secure cookies, and a small Redis-backed mechanism for revoking sessions. The approach can reduce database traffic significantly. But its security properties depend on how refresh tokens are managed, how revocation works, and which attacks the application needs to defend against. Let’s examine the architecture, its implementation in Node.js, and the trade-offs that are easy to overlook. 1. Why a Single Token Is Often Not Enough Consider an application that uses one JWT for authentication. After login, the server issues a token: Authorization : Bearer eyJhbGciOi... Every protected API request includes that token. The server verifies its signature and expiration time without querying a session database. This is convenient, but the token’s lifetime creates a problem. If it expires after 15 minutes, users need a way to obtain another token without repeatedly entering their credentials. If it remains valid for 30 days, stealing it may give an attacker access for a long time. Neither option is particularly attractive. What About Cookie-Based Sessions? Traditional session authentication usually stores an opaque session identifier in an HttpOnly cookie. The browser sends that cookie automatically, and the server looks up the associated session. This approach has important advantages. Tokens aren’t exposed to ordinary JavaScript through document.cookie , and individual sessions can be invalidated centrally. However, cookie-based authentication also requires appropriate CSRF defenses because browsers attach eligible cookies automatically. That doesn’t make cookie sessions inherently insecure. Properly implemented server-side sessions remain an excellent choice for many web applications. The question is whether the application needs the additional flexibility of separate access and refresh credentials. 2. Two Tokens, Two Responsibilities The Dual JWT approach separates API access from session renewal. Property Access token Refresh token Purpose Access protected APIs Obtain new access tokens Format JWT JWT in this design Lifetime 5–15 minutes Up to 30 days Transport Authorization header Secure cookie Client storage Memory HttpOnly cookie Verification Loca

articles.title: 科技爱好者周刊（第 421 期）：AI 的疯狂造富
articles.content: 这里记录每周值得分享的科技内容，周五发布。 本杂志 开源 ，欢迎 投稿 。另有 《谁在招人》 服务，发布程序员招聘信息。合作请 邮件联系 （ [email protected] ）。 封面图 本周，小鹏公司展示它的人形机器人。（ via ） AI 的疯狂造富 上周，模型公司 Anthropic 公司上市，创造出巨额财富。 这是一家历史很短的公司。它成立于2021年，当时规模很小，正式的大量对外招聘是2023年开始的。 大家知道吗，这么短的成立时间，又有这么高的估值，意味着什么？ 说得庸俗一点，就是加入这家公司，很快就能发大财。 根据 @AndrewBenson 的统计，截止今年9月底，它有约5300名员工，这些员工可以分到股票。 如果它的市值达到1.4万亿美元（目前是1.17万美元），这些员工的股票获利中位数是这样的。 2023年招聘的290人：1.51亿美元 2024年招聘的640人：7900万美元 2025年招聘的1360人：2600万美元 2026年招聘的3000人：500万美元 这很惊人，只要你在这家公司入职两年，就能拿到几千万美元。哪怕你今年年初才入职，几个月后就能拿到几百万美元。 这次上市一次性造就了600个亿万富翁，比洛杉矶全市现有的亿万富翁人数都多，而这些新的亿万富翁大部分只有二三十岁。 这些员工的财富都来自期权。加入越早，拿到的期权价格越低，份数越多。2024年授予的期权是每股1.30美元，上市后本周价格是每股80几美元。今年4月授予的期权则是每股25.91美元，只需持有半年，股价就变成3倍。 Anthropic 只是 AI 行业造富的一个典型例子。这种造富的规模和速度，前所未有。 美国的专栏作家 诺亚·史密斯 感叹，三年前和他一起聚餐的许多人，现在都通过 AI 行业变成了富豪，聚会地点变成了他们在旧金山山顶的那些装潢奢华、可以俯瞰壮丽海景的豪宅里。 你能想象这种感觉吗？曾经小酒馆里一起吃饭聊天的哥们，转眼三年后，财富就是你的成千上万倍，而他做的只是加入了一家 AI 公司。 这印证了流传已久的 IT 行业快速致富的两点秘诀。 （1） 加入一家即将上市的公司，拿到股权或期权 。只要在上市前加入都可以，但加入的最佳时间是上市的两年前。 （2） 这家公司的业务在上市时是业界热点 。这点至关重要，也就是所谓的"时势造英雄"，一定要选对方向。快速增长带来的机遇，是个人最大的托举，大于你自身的努力。要是选错方向，就算你真的有英雄的本领和刻苦的精神，也未必能出头。 维基百科的访问量 维基百科 公布 了来自真实人类的访问量。 疫情期间达到最高峰，此后有所下降，但保持平稳。2025年开始，就一路向下，目前已经创了新低。 要是维基百科都这样，中小网站的访问量惨到什么地步，就可想而知了。 现在架设个人网站，真的需要一点傻气，真人访问寥寥无几，流量都来自 AI 机器人。你掏自己的钱为服务器付费，结果就是免费向 AI 公司贡献内容，让他们的模型变得更好。 编程模型排名 一个国外程序员综合了 17 个编码基准测试，最后得到的 排名 。 前三名是 Fable 5.2、Astra 6.2、Neon 4。 国产模型排名最高的是 Qwen 4 Max（第10）、Kimi K3.1 Pro（第12）、Deepseek V.1 Flash（第14）。 个人感觉，可以用来参考。 科技动态 1、 防截图功能 微软和苹果都已经宣布，将自动对用户的屏幕进行截图，用来训练模型。这意味着，用户的电脑使用行为，有暴露和被监控的风险。 加密通信软件 Signal 因此推出了"防截图功能"，默认打开，操作系统将无法对它的窗口进行截图。 可以预料，会有越来越多的软件加入该功能。而且，因为 Linux 系统可能会变得更流行，因为它不会自动截图。 2、 重力通信 澳大利亚昆士兰大学的科学家，做了一个大开脑洞的实验。 他们让一部电梯在两层楼之间来回移动，同时改变这部电梯的配重。如果挂上1.8吨的钢块，就表示1，否则表示0。 这种电梯重量的变化，会被重力仪（下图）侦测到，从而得到二进制编码，完成通信。 这种通信的好处是无法屏蔽，因为重力场不可能被阻挡，从而可以用在传统通信手段失灵的隧道或山洞里。 缺点是需要非常灵敏的仪器才能捕捉到，而且通信速度极慢，每分钟传输一个比特（bit），传输一个单词需要1小时。 3、 手指鼠标 一家美国公司推出了戴在手指上的鼠标。 它的感应器紧贴手指正下方，当你移动食指，鼠标就会跟着动。如果敲击手指，鼠标就会点击。 它的最方便之处是，一侧有滚轮和5个自定义按钮，很多操作可以通过大拇指敲击食指来完成。 这种鼠标的优点是体积小，非常便携，缺点是不能装电池，必须插线使用。目前的定价是99美元，还是偏贵了一点。 文章 1、 我的天啊 x4 （英文） 最近几周，AI 公司连续发布重大的数学发现。数量之多，它们现在已经不发新闻稿了，直接把论文贴到 GitHub 上。甚至有传说，RSA 加密都被破解了。 这种进展使得著名的量子算法研究者 Scott Aaronson 都感到震惊，博客的标题就是连续4个"我的天啊"。 他对未来也感到不知所措，只能希望会变得更好。 2、 黄仁勋重返英伟达的 Polymarket 交易剖析 （英文） 有人在消息公布之前，就在预测市场 Ploymartket 上，买入看好黄仁勋回归的合约，结果一天获利14倍。 本文剖析这笔交易，可以从中了解 PolyMarket 的制度。我从中第一次知道，它的所有交易都是公开的，无法伪造。 3、 我不再把 SSH 私钥保存在磁盘上 （英文） 作者认为，SSH 私钥保存在个人磁盘上不安全，因此他把私钥保存在 Bitwarden，本文记录了他的具体做法。 4、 如何用 Unsloth 运行本地模型 （英文） Unsloth 是一个框架，可以压缩模型的显存开销。它有一个桌面客户端，用来将压缩后模型运行在本地，本文演示如何用它运行千问。 5、 CSS Mixin 之美 （英文） CSS 正在引入 Mixin 功能，也就是可以复用的 CSS 片段。本文提出，这个功能将改变 CSS 的编写方式。 6、 不用括号也能执行 JS 函数的一种方法 （英文） 本文介绍 JS 的一种高级技巧，如何不用括号来执行某个函数。 工具 1、 Ladybird Ladybird 是一个全新的开源浏览器，它的底层引擎是从头写的，跟市场上所有浏览器都不一样，是一个真正的独立替代方案。 本周，它发布了 alpha 版，也就是第一个可用版本（下图）。我推荐大家关注，它很可能将来会取代 Firefox 的位置。 2、 PenGPT 一个小型转换器（transformer），可以将英文输入转成手写字体，或者生成手绘草图。 3、 ScreenPlay 一款适用于 Windows 和 OSX 的开源动态壁纸应用。 4、 Plasmo 一个开发 Chrome 浏览器插件的框架。 5、 Trace 一个 macOS 菜单栏应用，自动记录你打开的应用、窗口、文件、网页，以及停留了多久，不需要手动计时。（ @lxyeternal 投稿） 6、 Uptime Polaris 开源的服务监控系统，检查网站是否在线，采集服务器

articles.title: 公司每个月只交 299 元公积金，剩下的都是我自己补的，一审法院却说这事不归法院管？
articles.content:
说一个最近遇到的事情，想看看 V 站有没有懂劳动法的朋友，或者有类似经历的。

之前在公司上班，公积金缴存基数按照实际工资计算，每个月应缴金额约 3240 元，但公司实际上每个月只承担 299 元，剩下的部分全部从我自己的工资里扣，相当于员工自己承担了大部分公积金缴存费用。

公积金账户看起来是足额缴纳的，但实际上公司并没有依法承担相应的缴存成本。

后来因为这个事情起诉，一审法院驳回了我的诉求，理由大致是认为住房公积金缴存问题属于公积金管理机构的行政管理职责，不属于法院民事案件的受理范围。

但问题恰恰就在这里。

我了解了一下公积金管理机构的处理方式，他们主要核查单位是否足额缴存。只要账户里的钱已经足额到账，通常就认为缴存没有问题。

但他们并不会进一步核查这笔钱到底是谁出的。

于是就出现了一个很奇怪的情况：

- 找法院，法院认为这属于公积金管理机构的职责；
- 找公积金管理机构，对方只看账户是否足额缴存；
- 账户虽然足额，但公司实际只承担了 299 元，剩下的都是员工自己承担。

这不就是典型的踢皮球吗？

法院和行政机构之间来回推，最后形成一个死循环。公司把本该自己承担的缴存义务转嫁给员工，员工却找不到一个真正解决这个问题的渠道。

我个人认为，这件事的核心并不只是公积金有没有足额缴纳，而是劳动关系存续期间，公司是否依法履行了应当由单位承担的缴存义务，以及是否存在将单位缴存成本转嫁给员工的行为。

从性质上看，这至少涉及劳动关系中的权利义务问题，理应有相应的劳动争议救济途径，而不能因为公积金账户已经足额到账，就忽略实际出资主体的问题。

想问问 V 站的朋友：

1. 这种公司只承担 299 元，剩余部分全部由员工工资承担的情况，究竟应该通过什么途径维权？
2. 这种争议是否可以作为劳动争议处理？
3. 有没有类似案例，法院最终支持员工要求公司返还其代为承担的单位缴存部分？

目前最困惑的就是，法院让我找公积金管理机构，公积金管理机构又解决不了资金实际由谁承担的问题。

难道这种事情最后就只能不了了之？

articles.title: 做了一个食品条码查询小程序，却发现产品推广比开发更难
articles.content:
最近做了个微信小程序，叫「咖态食品条码通」。

买食品的时候扫一下条形码，就能查商品信息、配料表和营养成分，还可以让 AI 帮忙解释那些看不懂的成分。


本来以为最难的是开发，结果发现最麻烦的是找数据，最难的是找用户。

小程序上线后试了知乎、短视频、微信群，折腾了一圈，推广效果也不怎么样。

现在 AI 编程这么方便，做个小程序确实不算太难，但做完之后怎么让别人知道，好像没什么特别好的办法。

于是最近又做了个网站，叫 MiniHunt（minihunt.top），想做一个专门发现微信小程序的地方，有点类似 Product Hunt。

自己有小程序的朋友可以免费发布，也可以看看其他独立开发者都在做什么。

不知道这个方向有没有价值，先做起来试试。

有没有同样在做小程序的朋友？想交流一下大家都是怎么找第一批用户的。

对了，食品扫码工具在微信里搜「咖态食品条码通」就能找到，有空可以帮忙试试。
articles.summary: 开发者做食品条码查询小程序，发现找数据和推广用户比开发更难，遂另建小程序发现站 MiniHunt。

articles.title: [推广] [发码] 做了个 AI 阅读器 ，我们想将 AI 和阅读器做深度结合，而不仅仅是简单问答
articles.content:
下面是我们已经做的 AI 功能，采用 BYOK 形式。

1. 阅读问答

读到不理解的词句，可以选中文字向 AI 提问。围绕原书内容随读随问，解释疑惑，帮助你理解正在阅读的内容。

2. 主动陪读

根据每本书的介入设置，在合适的时候提供续读回顾。当新读到的内容能够补充之前的问题时，也会适时给出跟进建议，帮助你衔接阅读思路。

3. 自动批注重点

阅读页面稳定后，AI 会复核少量关键原文，自动添加批注，并通过落笔动画呈现，帮助你抓住阅读重点。

4. 按策略标注

按照当前书籍的标注策略，自动标注当前可见原文中明确符合条件的内容，让阅读标记更贴合你的关注方向。

5. 双语阅读与翻译

生成并复核译文，辅助双语阅读，还可以提前翻译下一章，方便你在阅读原文时理解内容。

6. 导读与章节总结

生成导读、章节总结与相关学习内容，帮助你了解内容脉络、梳理章节重点，让阅读更有方向。

7. 书籍分析

分析书籍内容，推荐适合的阅读方式和辅助功能，帮助你判断这本书该怎么读、可以搭配哪些阅读工具。

8. 理解自检与练习

根据阅读内容生成自检问题与练习，检查理解情况，并提供批改反馈，帮助你发现尚未掌握的地方。

9. 书库助手

帮你查找书籍，并针对书库文件夹提出整理方案，让查书和整理书库更有条理。

10. 统一记录整理

检索并归纳已经保存的记录，整理阅读笔记，方便你回顾读过的内容与留下的想法。

11. 智能设置

通过文字或语音调整相关设置，也能解释 AI 用量，并打开需要你手动操作的配置卡片，让设置调整更方便。

12. 昨日总结

根据昨天实际阅读的内容与已保存的记录，生成阅读回顾，帮助你重新梳理昨日的重点与收获。

13. 今日发现

每天精选一篇与你阅读内容相关的外部文章，为阅读补充新的视角，发现值得继续了解的内容。

14. 自动长期记忆

从互动与阅读中自动提炼少量偏好，让后续提供的帮助更贴合你的阅读习惯与需求。

15. 扫描页面识别

使用支持视觉的 AI 模型识别扫描页面内容，为扫描版书籍的阅读提供辅助。

16. 智能朗读编排

提前判断人物与表达方式，配合调度可用声音，让朗读更贴合内容；播报过程不必等待 AI。

注：自动批注重点、按策略标注、智能朗读编排默认关闭，可按需开启。
articles.summary: 团队推出 BYOK 模式的 AI 阅读器，支持随读问答、主动陪读、自动批注和双语翻译等功能。

articles.title: 开启熊掌记网页版之旅
articles.content: 从创始之初，熊掌记的使命就是为你打造一个舒适而私密的空间，让你自在记录。但生活并不总是在自己的 Mac、iPhone 或 iPad 前展开，因此，我们一直在致力于让更多人在更多场景中使用熊掌记。今天，我们很高兴地宣布：熊掌记网页版正式上线啦！ 什么是熊掌记网页版？熊掌记网页版让你可以通过任何电脑上的浏览器查看、编辑和搜索笔记。它将同步你已有的笔记，界面也与 Mac 版熊掌记十分相似，让你从打开的第一刻起就倍感熟悉。随时随地访问笔记。 无论是在 Windows 或 Linux 电脑上、受 iCloud 使用限制的办公 Mac 上，还是旅行途中使用的笔记本电脑上，都能轻松使用熊掌记。延续未完成的工作。 继续编辑草稿、随手记录灵感，或搜索需要的笔记。所有修改都会在输入时自动保存至 iCloud。网络不稳定，也能继续写作。 在你信任的电脑上，熊掌记网页版会在浏览器中保存一份加密的笔记副本。即使网络中断，修改内容也不会丢失，待网络恢复后便会自动同步。一如既往地保护隐私。 你的笔记只会在浏览器和个人 iCloud 账号之间直接传输。我们不会存储你的笔记，也无法读取其中的内容。了解更多关于熊掌记网页版的隐私与安全。入门指南熊掌记网页版包含在最新版的 Bear Pro 订阅中。订阅后，只需按照以下步骤操作：确保 Mac、iPhone 或 iPad 上的熊掌记已通过 iCloud 同步笔记。打开 web.bear.app，点击「Sign in with Apple」（通过 Apple 登录）。使用与你的设备 iCloud 相同的 Apple 账号登录。如果登录窗口没有弹出，请在浏览器设置中允许 web.bear.app 打开弹出式窗口。完成！笔记将开始同步，你也可以开始写作了。使用须知熊掌记网页版包含在 2026 年 11 月 24 日及之后开通的 Bear Pro 订阅中。 如果你在此之前已订阅，可通过应用内的 Bear Pro 面板升级。了解新价格详情熊掌记网页版是原生应用的补充，并非替代品。 部分功能（如导出和加密笔记）目前尚不支持网页版，此外，网页版暂不兼容 Apple 高级数据保护（Advanced Data Protection）。查看使用要求与限制在自己的电脑上使用？ 将该设备设为可信设备，即可保持登录状态，即使离线也不用担心修改内容丢失。了解如何操作⠀还有其他疑问？欢迎查看熊掌记网页版 FAQ。开始体验！熊掌记网页版的推出是一个重要的新起点，我们非常期待你的使用和体验。若有任何反馈或 bug 报告，欢迎通过这里联系我们。你也可以在评论区留言分享你的想法，或直接发送邮件至 bear@shinyfrog.net。 祝您写作愉快！🐻❤️🕸️

articles.title: 大象漫步：一套键鼠控制你的所有设备
articles.content: 如果你桌上只有苹果全家桶，或者清一色都是华为、小米，其实很难理解多系统混用的人每天在烦什么。打开通用控制，光标顺着屏幕边缘滑进 iPad，一切自然得像本来就该这样。但我的桌子偏偏不是这样。平时写代码和主力折腾用着一台装了 Linux（niri 窗口管理器）的机器，手边摆着一台 Mac，旁边还有一台 Windows 用来测东西，再加上一台偶尔查资料、看文档的安卓平板和手机。四套系统挤在一张桌子上，硬件都是自己花钱买的，可每家厂商的多屏协同都把墙砌得死死的——苹果只认自家的，微软的无界鼠标只管 Windows，手机厂商的互联大多只认自家生态。这其实不是技术上做不到，而是大厂天然要把跨设备体验做成硬件护城河。可对普通用户来说，结果就是每天在键盘和鼠标之间反复抬手，或者为了把电脑上一张截图发到旁边的安卓平板，又点开微信文件传输助手给自己发一遍。试过一圈现成工具，最后还是卡在细节里在决定自己动手之前，我也用了很长一段时间现有的开源方案。最早是 Barrier，后来换到社区继续维护的 Deskflow，在 Linux Wayland 下也用过 Rust 写的 LAN Mouse。说实话，这几个项目都很优秀，如果只是两三台电脑之间互控，并且你希望软件完全开源可审计，现在直接选 Deskflow 或 LAN Mouse 依然是最稳妥的决定。真正让我每天用着别扭的，是几个看起来不大、但天天撞上的小毛病。第一个是换网就得重新折腾。电脑和笔记本偶尔切个 Wi-Fi，路由器重新分了局域网地址，原本连得好好的配置就断了，又得翻出来改 IP 和端口。第二个是屏幕比例对不上。我桌上有一块大显示器，旁边立着一块小得多的安卓平板。很多工具只认「左、右、上、下」四个方向，不认两块屏的真实物理尺寸，鼠标从大屏边缘滑过去，落点经常跳到莫名其妙的高度；更头疼的是平板一从横屏竖起来，原来对好的边缘全乱了。第三个最无解，就是安卓平板。Deskflow 这些传统软件 KVM 基本不原生支持安卓；用 scrcpy 虽然能把安卓画面投到电脑窗口里操作，但平板自己的屏幕反而成了摆设，而且我想做的是把鼠标直接滑进平板屏幕里打字、滚动、用触控板手势，顺便把文字和图片剪贴板双向打通。市面上的安卓输入方案，要么需要 Root，要么要折腾 Shizuku，总觉得门槛太高了一点。十月份的时候，我索性停下手头其他事，自己写了一套跨四端的局域网键鼠工具，取名叫「大象漫步」。自己动手以后，才发现「能连上」只是最容易的一步最开始在自己桌上跑通原型其实很快，真正耗掉大量时间的，是把那些平时容易被忽略的细节一点点磨顺。比如屏幕排列这件事。我不想让用户填像素或者记坐标，干脆直接按屏幕的真实物理毫米尺寸来画。在窗口里看到的每张卡片，大小比例都对应真实显示器和平板，拖动靠近另一块屏时会吸附对齐，只有真正贴在一起的绿边才能穿过，两个屏幕只是角对角擦到边不会误触。后来实测平板转屏时，又专门补了一条重锚规则：平板从横屏转成竖屏时，会死死贴住旁边邻居那条接缝往下沿对齐，而不是像很多工具那样直接重置回画布左上角。再比如安卓端怎么做到尽量不折腾。最终我选择了 Android 11 以后系统自带的无线调试机制来做一次性本机授权：不需要 Root，不需要装 Shizuku，也不用开无障碍服务或者挂一个常驻通知栏图标。授权完成后，电脑的键盘、鼠标、双指滚动和三指切换任务手势就能直接送进安卓系统，文字和图片剪贴板也是双向互通的。前两天刚把软件更新到 1.1.0，其实是被真实用户的网络环境逼出来的。在自己家里用同一台路由器，局域网广播发现一切顺利；可一旦拿去校园网、公司内网或者酒店 Wi-Fi，路由器开了 AP 隔离、禁了组播，设备之间直接成了孤岛。所以在 1.1.0 里，除了补上受限网络和代理环境下的连接兼容，我还给安卓加了 USB-C 数据线直连——遇到被隔离的 Wi-Fi，插上线就能自动完成免扫码授权和跨屏，不用再跟路由器较劲。聊两句绕不开的安全和边界做跨屏键鼠软件，只要主程序不是开源的，用户心里犯嘀咕太正常了——毕竟键盘输入和剪贴板里都是最私密的内容。我自己的底线很简单：所有键鼠操作、手势和剪贴板里的文字图片，全部只在你自己的局域网设备之间点对点传输，不经过任何云端服务器。具体实现上，控制和剪贴板通道走的是 TLS 1.3 双向证书认证并校验对端公钥指纹，高频鼠标移动数据报用会话导出的 AES-256-GCM 密钥单独加密防重放；软件本身也没有接任何行为统计或埋点。如果你不放心，直接开 Wireshark 或 Little Snitch 抓一下包，跨屏打字传图时能确认没有任何发往公网的数据流。当然，它现在也有非常明确的边界，说清楚免得大家白跑一趟：目前支持 Apple 芯片的 Mac（macOS 13 以上）、Window

articles.title: 让记账不再是负担：我做了一款安静的个人财务 App Flow
articles.content: 几乎每个想认真管钱的人，手机里都装过两三款记账 App。刚开始兴致勃勃：建好分类、录完余额、设好预算。但往往过不了两周，就会因为某天忘了记、周末懒得补，或者每次打开都要面对密密麻麻的报表和广告弹窗，最后把 App 塞进文件夹吃灰。做 Flow 的时候，我一直在想：一款个人财务工具，怎样才能既装得下日常流水、周期账单、预算、订阅和投资，又不会在不需要它的时候让人觉得有负担？Flow 是我用 SwiftUI 和 SwiftData 从零开发的原生个人财务 App，支持 iPhone、iPad 和 Apple Watch（Mac 版还在做）。它没有账号体系，没有社区和信息流，也没有广告，所有账目只保存在你的设备和你自己的 iCloud 里。这篇文章不打算罗列功能清单，而是想聊聊 Flow 在几个关键场景里的设计取舍。一、把「记一笔」的摩擦降到最低：最好根本不用打开 App记账失败的最大原因，往往不是懒，而是结账时那几秒钟的摩擦：你刚刷完卡，手里拎着咖啡，后面还有人在排队，这时候掏出手机、解锁、找 App、轻点加号、输金额、选账户，大概率会想「算了，晚上回家再记」，然后就没有然后了。所以 Flow 把重心放在了「无感」和「顺手」上。1. Apple Pay 自动记账：把系统自动化做成真正可用的功能Flow 借助快捷指令里的「交易」个人自动化：按 App 内的引导设置好之后，每次用 Apple Pay 付款，系统都会把金额、商户和卡片信息交给 Flow，在后台自动记成一笔支出。真正写代码时会发现，「自动记账」如果不处理边界情况，用起来反而更烦。所以我补齐了这几件事：通知上直接处理：记好之后会推送一条通知，带「改分类」和「撤销」两个按钮。不需要这笔的话，直接在通知上撤销，不用打开 App。不会悄悄丢单的「待确认」：没读出金额、遇到退款、用了一张新卡还没指定记到哪个账户，或者暂时没有对应币种的汇率，这笔都不会静默失败，而是进入「待确认」，等你轻点补全。防重复提醒：如果你在付款前后 10 分钟内已经手动记过一笔同币种、同金额的支出，Flow 会在通知里提示「可能重复」，可以直接删除这笔。2. Siri 快捷预设与 Apple WatchFlow 基于 App Intents 重新整理了记账预设。你可以提前把常用消费配好，比如「咖啡」「早餐」「通勤」，选好分类和账户，金额设为「固定金额」或「每次询问」。之后对 Siri 说「记账咖啡」，就能直接记一笔。Flow Pro 还提供 Apple Watch App，抬腕就能记账；主屏幕、锁定屏幕和控制中心也有对应的小组件和控制，从余额到快捷记账都能放在手边。3. 不打扰的记账提醒很多 App 的每日提醒像闹钟一样死板：不管你今天记没记，每晚八点准时弹一条「快来记账」。Flow 的记账提醒默认关闭，打开后遵循几条克制的规则：按你的习惯定时：记满 5 天后，按你平时记账的时间提醒；在那之前先在晚上 9:00 提醒。不想自动调整，也可以固定一个时间。记过就不提醒：当天已经记过账，就不会再打扰你。没理会就暂停：连续 3 次提醒都没有打开 Flow，提醒会自动暂停，下次打开 App 时再恢复。二、功能多与不复杂之间，隔着一个「简洁模式」最初规划时，我希望 Flow 是一个完整的个人财务中枢：交易流水、多账户资产、周期账单、预算、储蓄目标、投资组合、订阅管理……但不同阶段的我们需要不同的信息密度。有时你只想安安静静记个收支、看看账户余额；过几个月发了年终奖，又想把定投和净资产算清楚。于是我在设置里做了「简洁模式」：打开后只保留交易、资产和收支，计划、预算、投资和订阅全部收起，预算提醒也随之停止；它只是本机的显示开关，不会删除或改动任何数据，也不会同步到其他设备；哪天想做深度复盘了，随时关掉，所有设置和数据都原样还在。三、比「记下来」更进一步：计划、预算、储蓄、订阅与投资记账如果只停留在「知道钱花哪了」，成就感往往有限。Flow 在计划、预算、储蓄、订阅和投资上做了几个贴近真实生活的设计。1. 计划：把固定收支排进日历工资、房租、信用卡还款、保险，这些按月或按年固定发生的收支，在 Flow 里叫「计划」。计划页用日历排出每天的收入和支出，到期的项目会进入「待处理」：轻点「记一笔」就能入账，这次不需要的话也可以跳过。提前提醒：可以在当天，或提前 1 天、3 天、7 天提醒，时间自己定；到期日还可以添加到系统日历。自动执行：打开「自动执行」后，到期当天由 iPhone 自动记账。不用从零开始：「为你推荐」里有常用的计划模板，名称和分类自动填好，只需输入金额；Flow 还会根据历史交易，找出可能漏掉的计划。2. 按发薪日算预算，而不是死板的自然月很多人的房租、信用卡还款和生活费节奏，是跟着发薪日走的（比如每月 25 号到
